content.text: TFCC injuries are one of the most common causes of ulnar wrist pain.

items: FOOSH on an extended wrist
Rotational injury — wrist twisted into hypersupination
Repetitive ulnar deviation
Repetitive combined extension and pronation

content.text: The TFCC is poorly vascularised. This has implications for healing time (slow) and edema presentation (rare without combined injury such as fracture).

items: Deep ulnar-sided wrist pain
Worse with weight bearing on hands or carrying heavy objects (strong traction)
Pain or difficulty with end-range pronation, wrist extension, or ulnar deviation
Wrist may feel unstable

content.text: Edema following TFCC injury is rare and normally only occurs as a result of a combined injury (such as fracture with TFCC injury).

items: Did you hear a snap or pop?
Were you able to continue activity?
Does the wrist click, lock, or catch?
Does the wrist feel unstable? Are you able to bear weight through the wrist?
Did your wrist become swollen and if so, how badly and for how long?
AROM may provoke pain at end-range pronation and ulnar deviation
PROM: overpressure of pronation and ulnar deviation most likely to provoke
RROM may show weakness due to pain or inhibition

content.text: End range of radial deviation should NOT provoke pain in TFCC injury. If ulnar-sided wrist pain occurs with overpressure of radial deviation, it is more suggestive of an ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist sprain.

items: Muscle testing may be used to rule out injury to FCU or ECU
Ulnocarpal stress test is positive
Ulnar impaction test is positive
Ability to bear weight through the wrist is significantly reduced (e.g. leaning on hands, push-ups)
FCU or ECU tendinopathy
Ulnar impaction syndrome
Distal radioulnar sprains
Wrist support — braces or orthoses to offload the TFCC
TFCC is a slow-healing tissue — braces/splints may be needed for months
Once symptoms allow: ROM exercises, followed by gradual progressive strengthening
No particular muscle to emphasise — strengthen all muscles crossing the wrist
Most caution with: weight bearing, ulnar deviation, pronation, and extension

content.text: NSAIDs or corticosteroid injections may be prescribed. If conservative rehab is unsuccessful, surgery may be performed.

items: Restore neuromuscular control and resting muscle tone of the muscles around the joint
Restore normal range of motion of the wrist
Treat compensatory structures to restore overall function
Promote normal resting muscle tone of all muscles through the forearm
Decrease trigger point activity in the forearm and hand
Promote normal joint play with pain-free mid-range PROM of the wrist

content.title: Cautions
content.text: Avoid joint mobilisation if wrist is unstable. Do not perform axial compression or overpressure in ulnar deviation, extension, or pronation. Avoid joint play of the medial carpals. Use caution with distraction — if carrying heavy objects causes pain, do not attempt traction/distraction.
Prognosis for a TFCC injury is unclear and difficult to provide. Anecdotal experiences range from weeks to over a year of requiring joint support and activity modification.
Should include: onset (traumatic or gradual) and chronicity. Examples: 'Consistent with TFCC injury from traumatic onset since 6 weeks' or 'Consistent with gradual onset TFCC injury since 3 months.'

quiz.question: If ulnar-sided wrist pain occurs with overpressure of radial deviation, what does this suggest?
options: Ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist sprain
quiz.explanation: End range of radial deviation should NOT provoke pain in TFCC injury. If ulnar-sided wrist pain occurs with overpressure of radial deviation, it is more suggestive of an ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist sprain.

quiz.question: Which two special tests are positive in TFCC injury?
options: UCL stress test and grind test
Ulnocarpal stress test and ulnar impaction test
quiz.explanation: The ulnocarpal stress test and ulnar impaction test are positive in TFCC injury.

quiz.question: Significant edema is a common presentation of an isolated TFCC injury.
quiz.explanation: Edema following TFCC injury is rare and normally only occurs as a result of a combined injury such as a fracture with TFCC injury.
